extracted.intended_audience: advanced undergraduates, graduate students, and researchers in combinatorics/graph theory interested in topological and probabilistic proof techniques
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition and proof techniques in graph theory that use linear algebra, topology (Borsuk–Ulam / Lyusternik–Shnirel'man), eigenvalue methods, and the probabilistic method to obtain existence results and bounds (e.g., on Shannon capacity, chromatic number, Ramsey numbers, girth vs. chromatic number).

rubrics_metrics.name: Orthonormal representation via adjacency matrix
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a graph G with adjacency matrix A and smallest eigenvalue λm, set p = |λm| and M := I + (1/p) A. If M is real symmetric with all eigenvalues ≥ 0, then by the principal axis theorem there exist vectors v(1),…,v(m) such that mij = (v(i),v(j)) (1 ≤ i,j ≤ m). For M = I + (1/p)A this yields (v(i),v(i)) = 1 and (v(i),v(j)) = (1/p)aij for i ≠ j, so whenever aij = 0 the vectors form an orthonormal representation of G.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute eigenvalues of A to get p = |λmin|, form M = I + (1/p)A, apply the principal axis theorem to produce vectors whose inner products equal matrix entries; because aij = 0 for adjacent vertices this construction yields an orthonormal representation. This representation can be used to derive bounds on parameters like Θ(G) (Shannon capacity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Lovász umbrella / bound for Θ(G) (application to odd cycles)
rubrics_metrics.description: A larger σ^T (from an orthonormal representation) gives a better bound for Θ(G). Applying the orthonormal representation constructed from A to the m-cycle Cm (odd m ≥ 5) yields the bound (equation (9) in text) Θ(Cm) ≤ (1 + (cos(π/m))^{-1}).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute p = |λmin| for Cm (p = 2 cos(π/m)), obtain the representation and the inner products (v(i),u) = 1/m, then apply the main inequality (equation (8) in the book) to get the explicit upper bound. For m = 5 this recovers the classical Θ(C5) ≤ √5 bound (the Lovász result).

rubrics_metrics.name: Eigenvalues of cycle Cm via roots of unity
rubrics_metrics.description: For the adjacency matrix A of the cycle Cm (odd m), the eigenvalues are ζ^k + ζ^{-k} = 2 cos(2kπ/m) (0 ≤ k ≤ (m−1)/2). The smallest eigenvalue is −2 cos(π/m).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use m-th roots of unity ζ = e^{2πi/m}. The vector (1,λ,λ^2,…,λ^{m−1})^T is an eigenvector with eigenvalue λ + λ^{-1}; independence of these vectors (Vandermonde) gives the full spectrum. This eigenvalue information feeds into the orthonormal-representation construction above.

rubrics_metrics.name: Borsuk–Ulam theorem (continuous map antipodes)
rubrics_metrics.description: For every continuous map f : S^d → R^d there exist antipodal points x*, −x* with f(x*) = f(−x*).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a foundational topological result used to derive combinatorial existence statements. Many equivalent formulations exist; the book uses the theorem (and variants) to deduce antipodal coincidences from continuous maps constructed from combinatorial data (e.g., distance-to-set maps).

rubrics_metrics.name: Lyusternik–Shnirel'man covering theorem (antipodal version)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the d-sphere S^d is covered by d+1 sets S^d = U1 ∪ … ∪ Ud ∪ U_{d+1} where each of U1,…,Ud is either open or closed, then one of the d+1 sets contains a pair of antipodal points x*, −x*.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Borsuk–Ulam by mapping x ↦ (δ(x,U1),…,δ(x,Ud)) (distance vector) to R^d; continuity gives f, and Borsuk–Ulam yields antipodal equalities. The proof distinguishes whether Uk is open or closed and uses closure arguments for the open case. Greene's variant allows mixed open/closed among the first d sets and makes Ud+1 arbitrary for the Kneser application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gale's theorem (hemisphere point-counting)
rubrics_metrics.description: There exists an arrangement of 2k + d points on S^d such that every open hemisphere contains at least k of these points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Originally proved by Gale; such configurations can be explicitly constructed and are useful in topological-combinatorial proofs (e.g., of Kneser's conjecture). Greene observed that one can even avoid Gale's specific construction by taking points in general position on S^{d+1}.

rubrics_metrics.name: Greene simplification for Kneser proof (general-position points on S^{d+1})
rubrics_metrics.description: It suffices to take 2k + d points in general position on S^{d+1} (no d+2 points on a hyperplane through the center). For a partition of k-sets into d+1 classes, define for each class Vi the open set Oi of poles x whose open hemisphere H_x contains a k-set from Vi; the Oi's are open and together with the closed set C = S^{d+1}  igcup Oi cover the sphere. By Lyusternik–Shnirel'man some Oi contains antipodal points x*, −x*, whose hemispheres are disjoint and therefore yield two disjoint k-sets in the same class Vi.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provides the core topological argument proving the Kneser lower bound on chromatic number: antipodal hemispheres containing k-sets produce disjoint k-sets in the same color class, contradicting a coloring with too few colors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kneser conjecture (chromatic number of Kneser graphs)
rubrics_metrics.description: For n = 2k + d (k ≥ 1, d ≥ 0) the Kneser graph K(n,k) has chromatic number χ(K(2k+d,k)) = d + 2. An easy upper bound is given by coloring k-sets by their smallest element (d+2 colors); the nontrivial lower bound uses topological methods (Borsuk–Ulam / Lyusternik–Shnirel'man) to show any partition into d+1 classes yields a class containing two disjoint k-sets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prove upper bound by explicit coloring; prove lower bound by placing points on a sphere, defining hemisphere-based open sets for each color class, and invoking antipodal-point theorems to force a monochromatic pair of disjoint k-sets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Friendship theorem (unique politician / windmill graphs)
rubrics_metrics.description: If G is a finite graph in which any two vertices have precisely one common neighbor then there is a vertex adjacent to all other vertices (a 'politician'); the only such graphs are windmill graphs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof splits combinatorially and via linear algebra: (1) show G is k-regular and deduce n = k^2 − k + 1; (2) use the adjacency matrix A to compute A^2 = (k−1)I + J, deduce eigenvalues and multiplicities, and derive arithmetic contradictions (using rationality of square roots) unless graph is a windmill graph. This combines combinatorial counting and eigenvalue analysis as a blueprint for structural graph theorems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probabilistic method principle (existence via nonzero probability)
rubrics_metrics.description: If, in a given probability space on objects, the probability that an object does not have a certain property is less than 1, then there exists an object with that property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use random constructions and compute probabilities (often via union bound, linearity of expectation, Markov's inequality) to show existence of combinatorial structures. The chapter gives standard templates (random colorings, random graphs G(n,p)) and specific worked examples (2-colorability thresholds, Ramsey lower bounds, graphs with large girth and high chromatic number).

rubrics_metrics.name: 2-colorability bound for families of d-sets (m(d) > 2^{d-1})
rubrics_metrics.description: Every family of at most 2^{d−1} d-sets is 2-colorable. Randomly color the ground set with two colors; for each d-set A the probability all elements are same color is 2^{-(d-1)}. Summing probabilities over m ≤ 2^{d−1} sets gives total < 1, guaranteeing a 2-coloring with no monochromatic d-set.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the union bound (Boole's inequality) to events that a given d-set is monochromatic. This is the prototype probabilistic existence proof via expectation/union bound.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ramsey recursion and upper bound
rubrics_metrics.description: Recurrence: R(m,n) ≤ R(m−1,n) + R(m,n−1). Starting values R(m,2)=m and R(2,n)=n yield the binomial upper bound R(m,n) ≤ C(m+n−2,m−1) and in particular R(k,k) ≤ C(2k−2,k−1) ≤ 2^{2k−3}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the standard vertex-splitting argument: consider degrees to red or blue neighbors of a chosen vertex and apply inductive hypothesis. Translate recursion into combinatorial binomial bounds for explicit asymptotics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probabilistic lower bound for Ramsey numbers (Erdős)
rubrics_metrics.description: For k ≥ 2, R(k,k) ≥ 2^{k/2}. Consider random red/blue edge-coloring with each edge independently red or blue with probability 1/2; compute probability some k-set is monochromatic (2·C(N,k)·2^{−C(k,2)}). For N < 2^{k/2} this probability < 1, so a coloring exists without monochromatic K_k.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Count number of k-sets and the probability each is monochromatic; apply union bound. This yields the well-known exponential lower bound on diagonal Ramsey numbers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence of graphs with large girth and chromatic number via G(n,p)
rubrics_metrics.description: For any fixed k ≥ 2, there exist graphs G with χ(G) > k and girth γ(G) > k. Choose n large and p = n^{−1/(k+1)}. Show Prob(α(G) ≥ n/(2k)) < 1/2 (so independence number small → chromatic number large) and Prob(number of cycles of length ≤ k ≥ n/2) < 1/2 (so few short cycles). Deleting one vertex from each short cycle yields a graph with girth > k and still large chromatic number.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use bounds on Prob(a given r-set is independent) = (1−p)^{C(r,2)}, union bound and exponential estimates (1−p ≤ e^{−p}) to bound Prob(α large). For cycles use linearity of expectation and Markov's inequality. This template (choose p, bound independence and short-cycle counts, then modify) is standard for probabilistic existence of extreme graphs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counting cycles and Markov/expectation technique
rubrics_metrics.description: To bound the expected number of cycles of length ≤ k in G(n,p), sum expectations of indicator variables for each possible cycle: E[X] = Σ (number_of_possible_i_cycles) p^i ≤ 1/2 (k−2) n p^k. Then apply Markov's inequality: Prob(X ≥ a) ≤ E[X]/a.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the standard way to show that with positive probability a random graph has few short cycles (so high girth after small vertex deletions). Combine with bounds on independence number to get the desired structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimal crossing drawing constraints (crossing number)
rubrics_metrics.description: In a drawing of a graph that achieves the crossing number (minimal number of edge crossings), these situations are ruled out: (i) no edge crosses itself; (ii) edges with a common endvertex do not cross; (iii) no two edges cross twice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When arguing about minimal crossing drawings one may assume these three local minimality conditions, since any drawing violating them can be locally modified to reduce crossings. These are useful preconditions when deriving global lower bounds on crossing numbers.
